lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: X. THE ADVENTURE OF THE NOBLE BACHELOR

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Lord St. Simon marriage, and its curious termination, have long ceased to be a subject of interest in those exalted circles in which the unfortunate bridegroom moves. Fresh scandals have eclipsed it, and their more piquant details have drawn the gossips away from this four-year-old drama. As I have reason to believe, however, that the full facts have never been revealed to the general public, and as my friend Sherlock Holmes had a considerable share in clearing the matter up, I feel that no memoir of him would be complete without some little sketch of this remarkable episode.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was a few weeks before my own marriage, during the days when I was still sharing rooms with Holmes in Baker Street, that he came home from an afternoon stroll to find a letter on the table waiting for him. I had remained indoors all day, for the weather had taken a sudden turn to rain, with high autumnal winds, and the jezail bullet which I had brought back in one of my limbs as a relic of my Afghan campaign throbbed with dull persistence. With my body in one easy-chair and my legs upon another, I had surrounded myself with a cloud of newspapers until at last, saturated with the news of the day, I tossed them all aside and lay listless, watching the huge crest and monogram upon the envelope upon the table and wondering lazily who my friend’s noble correspondent could be.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Here is a very fashionable epistle,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: I remarked as he entered.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Your morning letters, if I remember right, were from a fish-monger and a tide-waiter.”

lines.speaker: Mr. Baker
lines.text: “Yes, my correspondence has certainly the charm of variety,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he answered, smiling,

lines.speaker: Mr. Baker
lines.text: “and the humbler are usually the more interesting. This looks like one of those unwelcome social summonses which call upon a man either to be bored or to lie.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He broke the seal and glanced over the contents.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Oh, come, it may prove to be something of interest, after all.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Not social, then?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “No, distinctly professional.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “And from a noble client?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “One of the highest in England.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “My dear fellow, I congratulate you.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I assure you, Watson, without affectation, that the status of my client is a matter of less moment to me than the interest of his case. It is just possible, however, that that also may not be wanting in this new investigation. You have been reading the papers diligently of late, have you not?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “It looks like it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said I ruefully, pointing to a huge bundle in the corner.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I have had nothing else to do.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “It is fortunate, for you will perhaps be able to post me up. I read nothing except the criminal news and the agony column. The latter is always instructive. But if you have followed recent events so closely you must have read about Lord St. Simon and his wedding?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Oh, yes, with the deepest interest.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “That is well. The letter which I hold in my hand is from Lord St. Simon. I will read it to you, and in return you must turn over these papers and let me have whatever bears upon the matter. This is what he says:”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “‘MY DEAR MR. SHERLOCK HOLMES,—Lord Backwater tells me that I may place implicit reliance upon your judgment and discretion. I have determined, therefore, to call upon you and to consult you in reference to the very painful event which has occurred in connection with my wedding. Mr. Lestrade, of Scotland Yard, is acting already in the matter, but he assures me that he sees no objection to your co-operation, and that he even thinks that it might be of some assistance. I will call at four o’clock in the afternoon, and, should you have any other engagement at that time, I hope that you will postpone it, as this matter is of paramount importance. Yours faithfully,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “‘ROBERT ST. SIMON.’”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “It is dated from Grosvenor Mansions, written with a quill pen, and the noble lord has had the misfortune to get a smear of ink upon the outer side of his right little finger,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: remarked Holmes as he folded up the epistle.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “He says four o’clock. It is three now. He will be here in an hour.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Then I have just time, with your assistance, to get clear upon the subject. Turn over those papers and arrange the extracts in their order of time, while I take a glance as to who our client is.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He picked a red-covered volume from a line of books of reference beside the mantelpiece.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Here he is,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he, sitting down and flattening it out upon his knee.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “‘Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon, second son of the Duke of Balmoral.’ Hum! ‘Arms: Azure, three caltrops in chief over a fess sable. Born in 1846.’ He’s forty-one years of age, which is mature for marriage. Was Under-Secretary for the colonies in a late administration. The Duke, his father, was at one time Secretary for Foreign Affairs. They inherit Plantagenet blood by direct descent, and Tudor on the distaff side. Ha! Well, there is nothing very instructive in all this. I think that I must turn to you Watson, for something more solid.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I have very little difficulty in finding what I want,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said I,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “for the facts are quite recent, and the matter struck me as remarkable. I feared to refer them to you, however, as I knew that you had an inquiry on hand and that you disliked the intrusion of other matters.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Oh, you mean the little problem of the Grosvenor Square furniture van. That is quite cleared up now—though, indeed, it was obvious from the first. Pray give me the results of your newspaper selections.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Here is the first notice which I can find. It is in the personal column of the Morning Post, and dates, as you see, some weeks back: ‘A marriage has been arranged,’ it says, ‘and will, if rumour is correct, very shortly take place, between Lord Robert St. Simon, second son of the Duke of Balmoral, and Miss Hatty Doran, the only daughter of Aloysius Doran. Esq., of San Francisco, Cal., U.S.A.’ That is all.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Terse and to the point,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: remarked Holmes, stretching his long, thin legs towards the fire.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “There was a paragraph amplifying this in one of the society papers of the same week. Ah, here it is: ‘There will soon be a call for protection in the marriage market, for the present free-trade principle appears to tell heavily against our home product. One by one the management of the noble houses of Great Britain is passing into the hands of our fair cousins from across the Atlantic. An important addition has been made during the last week to the list of the prizes which have been borne away by these charming invaders. Lord St. Simon, who has shown himself for over twenty years proof against the little god’s arrows, has now definitely announced his approaching marriage with Miss Hatty Doran, the fascinating daughter of a California millionaire. Miss Doran, whose graceful figure and striking face attracted much attention at the Westbury House festivities, is an only child, and it is currently reported that her dowry will run to considerably over the six figures, with expectancies for the future. As it is an open secret that the Duke of Balmoral has been compelled to sell his pictures within the last few years, and as Lord St. Simon has no property of his own save the small estate of Birchmoor, it is obvious that the Californian heiress is not the only gainer by an alliance which will enable her to make the easy and common transition from a Republican lady to a British peeress.’”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Anything else?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Holmes, yawning.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Oh, yes; plenty. Then there is another note in the Morning Post to say that the marriage would be an absolutely quiet one, that it would be at St. George’s, Hanover Square, that only half a dozen intimate friends would be invited, and that the party would return to the furnished house at Lancaster Gate which has been taken by Mr. Aloysius Doran. Two days later—that is, on Wednesday last—there is a curt announcement that the wedding had taken place, and that the honeymoon would be passed at Lord Backwater’s place, near Petersfield. Those are all the notices which appeared before the disappearance of the bride.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Before the what?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Holmes with a start.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “The vanishing of the lady.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “When did she vanish, then?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “At the wedding breakfast.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Indeed. This is more interesting than it promised to be; quite dramatic, in fact.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes; it struck me as being a little out of the common.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “They often vanish before the ceremony, and occasionally during the honeymoon; but I cannot call to mind anything quite so prompt as this. Pray let me have the details.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I warn you that they are very incomplete.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Perhaps we may make them less so.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Such as they are, they are set forth in a single article of a morning paper of yesterday, which I will read to you. It is headed, ‘Singular Occurrence at a Fashionable Wedding’:”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “‘The family of Lord Robert St. Simon has been thrown into the greatest consternation by the strange and painful episodes which have taken place in connection with his wedding. The ceremony, as shortly announced in the papers of yesterday, occurred on the previous morning; but it is only now that it has been possible to confirm the strange rumours which have been so persistently floating about. In spite of the attempts of the friends to hush the matter up, so much public attention has now been drawn to it that no good purpose can be served by affecting to disregard what is a common subject for conversation.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “‘The ceremony, which was performed at St. George’s, Hanover Square, was a very quiet one, no one being present save the father of the bride, Mr. Aloysius Doran, the Duchess of Balmoral, Lord Backwater, Lord Eustace and Lady Clara St. Simon (the younger brother and sister of the bridegroom), and Lady Alicia Whittington. The whole party proceeded afterwards to the house of Mr. Aloysius Doran, at Lancaster Gate, where breakfast had been prepared. It appears that some little trouble was caused by a woman, whose name has not been ascertained, who endeavoured to force her way into the house after the bridal party, alleging that she had some claim upon Lord St. Simon. It was only after a painful and prolonged scene that she was ejected by the butler and the footman. The bride, who had fortunately entered the house before this unpleasant interruption, had sat down to breakfast with the rest, when she complained of a sudden indisposition and retired to her room. Her prolonged absence having caused some comment, her father followed her, but learned from her maid that she had only come up to her chamber for an instant, caught up an ulster and bonnet, and hurried down to the passage. One of the footmen declared that he had seen a lady leave the house thus apparelled, but had refused to credit that it was his mistress, believing her to be with the company. On ascertaining that his daughter had disappeared, Mr. Aloysius Doran, in conjunction with the bridegroom, instantly put themselves in communication with the police, and very energetic inquiries are being made, which will probably result in a speedy clearing up of this very singular business. Up to a late hour last night, however, nothing had transpired as to the whereabouts of the missing lady. There are rumours of foul play in the matter, and it is said that the police have caused the arrest of the woman who had caused the original disturbance, in the belief that, from jealousy or some other motive, she may have been concerned in the strange disappearance of the bride.’”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “And is that all?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Only one little item in another of the morning papers, but it is a suggestive one.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “And it is—”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “That Miss Flora Millar, the lady who had caused the disturbance, has actually been arrested. It appears that she was formerly a danseuse at the Allegro, and that she has known the bridegroom for some years. There are no further particulars, and the whole case is in your hands now—so far as it has been set forth in the public press.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “And an exceedingly interesting case it appears to be. I would not have missed it for worlds. But there is a ring at the bell, Watson, and as the clock makes it a few minutes after four, I have no doubt that this will prove to be our noble client. Do not dream of going, Watson, for I very much prefer having a witness, if only as a check to my own memory.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Lord Robert St. Simon,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: announced our page-boy, throwing open the door. A gentleman entered, with a pleasant, cultured face, high-nosed and pale, with something perhaps of petulance about the mouth, and with the steady, well-opened eye of a man whose pleasant lot it had ever been to command and to be obeyed. His manner was brisk, and yet his general appearance gave an undue impression of age, for he had a slight forward stoop and a little bend of the knees as he walked. His hair, too, as he swept off his very curly-brimmed hat, was grizzled round the edges and thin upon the top. As to his dress, it was careful to the verge of foppishness, with high collar, black frock-coat, white waistcoat, yellow gloves, patent-leather shoes, and light-coloured gaiters. He advanced slowly into the room, turning his head from left to right, and swinging in his right hand the cord which held his golden eyeglasses.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Good-day, Lord St. Simon,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes, rising and bowing.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Pray take the basket-chair. This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson. Draw up a little to the fire, and we will talk this matter over.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “A most painful matter to me, as you can most readily imagine, Mr. Holmes. I have been cut to the quick. I understand that you have already managed several delicate cases of this sort, sir, though I presume that they were hardly from the same class of society.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “No, I am descending.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I beg pardon.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “My last client of the sort was a king.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Oh, really! I had no idea. And which king?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “The King of Scandinavia.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “What! Had he lost his wife?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You can understand,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes suavely,

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “that I extend to the affairs of my other clients the same secrecy which I promise to you in yours.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Of course! Very right! very right! I’m sure I beg pardon. As to my own case, I am ready to give you any information which may assist you in forming an opinion.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Thank you. I have already learned all that is in the public prints, nothing more. I presume that I may take it as correct—this article, for example, as to the disappearance of the bride.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lord St. Simon glanced over it.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes, it is correct, as far as it goes.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “But it needs a great deal of supplementing before anyone could offer an opinion. I think that I may arrive at my facts most directly by questioning you.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Pray do so.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “When did you first meet Miss Hatty Doran?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “In San Francisco, a year ago.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You were travelling in the States?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Did you become engaged then?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “No.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “But you were on a friendly footing?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I was amused by her society, and she could see that I was amused.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Her father is very rich?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “He is said to be the richest man on the Pacific slope.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And how did he make his money?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “In mining. He had nothing a few years ago. Then he struck gold, invested it, and came up by leaps and bounds.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Now, what is your own impression as to the young lady’s—your wife’s character?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The nobleman swung his glasses a little faster and stared down into the fire.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “You see, Mr. Holmes,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he,

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “my wife was twenty before her father became a rich man. During that time she ran free in a mining camp and wandered through woods or mountains, so that her education has come from Nature rather than from the schoolmaster. She is what we call in England a tomboy, with a strong nature, wild and free, unfettered by any sort of traditions. She is impetuous—volcanic, I was about to say. She is swift in making up her mind and fearless in carrying out her resolutions. On the other hand, I would not have given her the name which I have the honour to bear”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: —he gave a little stately cough—

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “had I not thought her to be at bottom a noble woman. I believe that she is capable of heroic self-sacrifice and that anything dishonourable would be repugnant to her.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Have you her photograph?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I brought this with me.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He opened a locket and showed us the full face of a very lovely woman. It was not a photograph but an ivory miniature, and the artist had brought out the full effect of the lustrous black hair, the large dark eyes, and the exquisite mouth. Holmes gazed long and earnestly at it. Then he closed the locket and handed it back to Lord St. Simon.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “The young lady came to London, then, and you renewed your acquaintance?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes, her father brought her over for this last London season. I met her several times, became engaged to her, and have now married her.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “She brought, I understand, a considerable dowry?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “A fair dowry. Not more than is usual in my family.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And this, of course, remains to you, since the marriage is a fait accompli?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I really have made no inquiries on the subject.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Very naturally not. Did you see Miss Doran on the day before the wedding?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Was she in good spirits?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Never better. She kept talking of what we should do in our future lives.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Indeed! That is very interesting. And on the morning of the wedding?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “She was as bright as possible—at least until after the ceremony.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And did you observe any change in her then?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Well, to tell the truth, I saw then the first signs that I had ever seen that her temper was just a little sharp. The incident however, was too trivial to relate and can have no possible bearing upon the case.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Pray let us have it, for all that.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Oh, it is childish. She dropped her bouquet as we went towards the vestry. She was passing the front pew at the time, and it fell over into the pew. There was a moment’s delay, but the gentleman in the pew handed it up to her again, and it did not appear to be the worse for the fall. Yet when I spoke to her of the matter, she answered me abruptly; and in the carriage, on our way home, she seemed absurdly agitated over this trifling cause.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Indeed! You say that there was a gentleman in the pew. Some of the general public were present, then?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Oh, yes. It is impossible to exclude them when the church is open.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “This gentleman was not one of your wife’s friends?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “No, no; I call him a gentleman by courtesy, but he was quite a common-looking person. I hardly noticed his appearance. But really I think that we are wandering rather far from the point.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Lady St. Simon, then, returned from the wedding in a less cheerful frame of mind than she had gone to it. What did she do on re-entering her father’s house?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I saw her in conversation with her maid.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And who is her maid?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Alice is her name. She is an American and came from California with her.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “A confidential servant?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “A little too much so. It seemed to me that her mistress allowed her to take great liberties. Still, of course, in America they look upon these things in a different way.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “How long did she speak to this Alice?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Oh, a few minutes. I had something else to think of.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You did not overhear what they said?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Lady St. Simon said something about ‘jumping a claim.’ She was accustomed to use slang of the kind. I have no idea what she meant.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “American slang is very expressive sometimes. And what did your wife do when she finished speaking to her maid?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “She walked into the breakfast-room.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “On your arm?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “No, alone. She was very independent in little matters like that. Then, after we had sat down for ten minutes or so, she rose hurriedly, muttered some words of apology, and left the room. She never came back.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “But this maid, Alice, as I understand, deposes that she went to her room, covered her bride’s dress with a long ulster, put on a bonnet, and went out.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Quite so. And she was afterwards seen walking into Hyde Park in company with Flora Millar, a woman who is now in custody, and who had already made a disturbance at Mr. Doran’s house that morning.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Ah, yes. I should like a few particulars as to this young lady, and your relations to her.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lord St. Simon shrugged his shoulders and raised his eyebrows.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “We have been on a friendly footing for some years—I may say on a very friendly footing. She used to be at the Allegro. I have not treated her ungenerously, and she had no just cause of complaint against me, but you know what women are, Mr. Holmes. Flora was a dear little thing, but exceedingly hot-headed and devotedly attached to me. She wrote me dreadful letters when she heard that I was about to be married, and, to tell the truth, the reason why I had the marriage celebrated so quietly was that I feared lest there might be a scandal in the church. She came to Mr. Doran’s door just after we returned, and she endeavoured to push her way in, uttering very abusive expressions towards my wife, and even threatening her, but I had foreseen the possibility of something of the sort, and I had two police fellows there in private clothes, who soon pushed her out again. She was quiet when she saw that there was no good in making a row.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Did your wife hear all this?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “No, thank goodness, she did not.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And she was seen walking with this very woman afterwards?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Yes. That is what Mr. Lestrade, of Scotland Yard, looks upon as so serious. It is thought that Flora decoyed my wife out and laid some terrible trap for her.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Well, it is a possible supposition.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “You think so, too?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I did not say a probable one. But you do not yourself look upon this as likely?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I do not think Flora would hurt a fly.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Still, jealousy is a strange transformer of characters. Pray what is your own theory as to what took place?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Well, really, I came to seek a theory, not to propound one. I have given you all the facts. Since you ask me, however, I may say that it has occurred to me as possible that the excitement of this affair, the consciousness that she had made so immense a social stride, had the effect of causing some little nervous disturbance in my wife.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “In short, that she had become suddenly deranged?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Well, really, when I consider that she has turned her back—I will not say upon me, but upon so much that many have aspired to without success—I can hardly explain it in any other fashion.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Well, certainly that is also a conceivable hypothesis,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes, smiling.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And now, Lord St. Simon, I think that I have nearly all my data. May I ask whether you were seated at the breakfast-table so that you could see out of the window?”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “We could see the other side of the road and the Park.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Quite so. Then I do not think that I need to detain you longer. I shall communicate with you.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Should you be fortunate enough to solve this problem,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said our client, rising.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I have solved it.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Eh? What was that?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I say that I have solved it.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Where, then, is my wife?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “That is a detail which I shall speedily supply.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lord St. Simon shook his head.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I am afraid that it will take wiser heads than yours or mine,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he remarked, and bowing in a stately, old-fashioned manner he departed.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “It is very good of Lord St. Simon to honour my head by putting it on a level with his own,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Sherlock Holmes, laughing.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I think that I shall have a whisky and soda and a cigar after all this cross-questioning. I had formed my conclusions as to the case before our client came into the room.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “My dear Holmes!”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I have notes of several similar cases, though none, as I remarked before, which were quite as prompt. My whole examination served to turn my conjecture into a certainty. Circumstantial evidence is occasionally very convincing, as when you find a trout in the milk, to quote Thoreau’s example.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “But I have heard all that you have heard.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Without, however, the knowledge of pre-existing cases which serves me so well. There was a parallel instance in Aberdeen some years back, and something on very much the same lines at Munich the year after the Franco-Prussian War. It is one of these cases—but, hullo, here is Lestrade! Good-afternoon, Lestrade! You will find an extra tumbler upon the sideboard, and there are cigars in the box.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which gave him a decidedly nautical appearance, and he carried a black canvas bag in his hand. With a short greeting he seated himself and lit the cigar which had been offered to him.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “What’s up, then?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Holmes with a twinkle in his eye.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You look dissatisfied.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “And I feel dissatisfied. It is this infernal St. Simon marriage case. I can make neither head nor tail of the business.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Really! You surprise me.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Who ever heard of such a mixed affair? Every clue seems to slip through my fingers. I have been at work upon it all day.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And very wet it seems to have made you,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes laying his hand upon the arm of the pea-jacket.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Yes, I have been dragging the Serpentine.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “In Heaven’s name, what for?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “In search of the body of Lady St. Simon.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Sherlock Holmes leaned back in his chair and laughed heartily.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Have you dragged the basin of Trafalgar Square fountain?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he asked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Why? What do you mean?”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Because you have just as good a chance of finding this lady in the one as in the other.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lestrade shot an angry glance at my companion.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I suppose you know all about it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he snarled.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Well, I have only just heard the facts, but my mind is made up.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Oh, indeed! Then you think that the Serpentine plays no part in the matter?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I think it very unlikely.”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Then perhaps you will kindly explain how it is that we found this in it?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He opened his bag as he spoke, and tumbled onto the floor a wedding-dress of watered silk, a pair of white satin shoes and a bride’s wreath and veil, all discoloured and soaked in water.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “There,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he, putting a new wedding-ring upon the top of the pile.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “There is a little nut for you to crack, Master Holmes.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Oh, indeed!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said my friend, blowing blue rings into the air.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You dragged them from the Serpentine?”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “No. They were found floating near the margin by a park-keeper. They have been identified as her clothes, and it seemed to me that if the clothes were there the body would not be far off.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “By the same brilliant reasoning, every man’s body is to be found in the neighbourhood of his wardrobe. And pray what did you hope to arrive at through this?”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “At some evidence implicating Flora Millar in the disappearance.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I am afraid that you will find it difficult.”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Are you, indeed, now?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Lestrade with some bitterness.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “I am afraid, Holmes, that you are not very practical with your deductions and your inferences. You have made two blunders in as many minutes. This dress does implicate Miss Flora Millar.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And how?”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “In the dress is a pocket. In the pocket is a card-case. In the card-case is a note. And here is the very note.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He slapped it down upon the table in front of him.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Listen to this: ‘You will see me when all is ready. Come at once. F. H. M.’ Now my theory all along has been that Lady St. Simon was decoyed away by Flora Millar, and that she, with confederates, no doubt, was responsible for her disappearance. Here, signed with her initials, is the very note which was no doubt quietly slipped into her hand at the door and which lured her within their reach.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Very good, Lestrade,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes, laughing.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You really are very fine indeed. Let me see it.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He took up the paper in a listless way, but his attention instantly became riveted, and he gave a little cry of satisfaction.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “This is indeed important,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “Ha! you find it so?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Extremely so. I congratulate you warmly.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lestrade rose in his triumph and bent his head to look.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Why,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he shrieked,

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “you’re looking at the wrong side!”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “On the contrary, this is the right side.”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “The right side? You’re mad! Here is the note written in pencil over here.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “And over here is what appears to be the fragment of a hotel bill, which interests me deeply.”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “There’s nothing in it. I looked at it before,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Lestrade.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “‘Oct. 4th, rooms 8s., breakfast 2s. 6d., cocktail 1s., lunch 2s. 6d., glass sherry, 8d.’ I see nothing in that.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Very likely not. It is most important, all the same. As to the note, it is important also, or at least the initials are, so I congratulate you again.”

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “I’ve wasted time enough,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Lestrade, rising.

lines.speaker: Lestrade
lines.text: “I believe in hard work and not in sitting by the fire spinning fine theories. Good-day, Mr. Holmes, and we shall see which gets to the bottom of the matter first.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He gathered up the garments, thrust them into the bag, and made for the door.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Just one hint to you, Lestrade,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: drawled Holmes before his rival vanished;

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I will tell you the true solution of the matter. Lady St. Simon is a myth. There is not, and there never has been, any such person.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lestrade looked sadly at my companion. Then he turned to me, tapped his forehead three times, shook his head solemnly, and hurried away.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He had hardly shut the door behind him when Holmes rose to put on his overcoat.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “There is something in what the fellow says about outdoor work,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he remarked,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “so I think, Watson, that I must leave you to your papers for a little.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was after five o’clock when Sherlock Holmes left me, but I had no time to be lonely, for within an hour there arrived a confectioner’s man with a very large flat box. This he unpacked with the help of a youth whom he had brought with him, and presently, to my very great astonishment, a quite epicurean little cold supper began to be laid out upon our humble lodging-house mahogany. There were a couple of brace of cold woodcock, a pheasant, a pâté de foie gras pie with a group of ancient and cobwebby bottles. Having laid out all these luxuries, my two visitors vanished away, like the genii of the Arabian Nights, with no explanation save that the things had been paid for and were ordered to this address.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Just before nine o’clock Sherlock Holmes stepped briskly into the room. His features were gravely set, but there was a light in his eye which made me think that he had not been disappointed in his conclusions.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “They have laid the supper, then,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said, rubbing his hands.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “You seem to expect company. They have laid for five.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Yes, I fancy we may have some company dropping in,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I am surprised that Lord St. Simon has not already arrived. Ha! I fancy that I hear his step now upon the stairs.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was indeed our visitor of the afternoon who came bustling in, dangling his glasses more vigorously than ever, and with a very perturbed expression upon his aristocratic features.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “My messenger reached you, then?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Holmes.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Yes, and I confess that the contents startled me beyond measure. Have you good authority for what you say?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “The best possible.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lord St. Simon sank into a chair and passed his hand over his forehead.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “What will the Duke say,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he murmured,

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “when he hears that one of the family has been subjected to such humiliation?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “It is the purest accident. I cannot allow that there is any humiliation.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Ah, you look on these things from another standpoint.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I fail to see that anyone is to blame. I can hardly see how the lady could have acted otherwise, though her abrupt method of doing it was undoubtedly to be regretted. Having no mother, she had no one to advise her at such a crisis.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “It was a slight, sir, a public slight,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Lord St. Simon, tapping his fingers upon the table.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “You must make allowance for this poor girl, placed in so unprecedented a position.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I will make no allowance. I am very angry indeed, and I have been shamefully used.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I think that I heard a ring,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Yes, there are steps on the landing. If I cannot persuade you to take a lenient view of the matter, Lord St. Simon, I have brought an advocate here who may be more successful.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He opened the door and ushered in a lady and gentleman.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Lord St. Simon,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said he

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “allow me to introduce you to Mr. and Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton. The lady, I think, you have already met.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At the sight of these newcomers our client had sprung from his seat and stood very erect, with his eyes cast down and his hand thrust into the breast of his frock-coat, a picture of offended dignity. The lady had taken a quick step forward and had held out her hand to him, but he still refused to raise his eyes. It was as well for his resolution, perhaps, for her pleading face was one which it was hard to resist.

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “You’re angry, Robert,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said she.

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Well, I guess you have every cause to be.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Pray make no apology to me,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Lord St. Simon bitterly.

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Oh, yes, I know that I have treated you real bad and that I should have spoken to you before I went; but I was kind of rattled, and from the time when I saw Frank here again I just didn’t know what I was doing or saying. I only wonder I didn’t fall down and do a faint right there before the altar.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “Perhaps, Mrs. Moulton, you would like my friend and me to leave the room while you explain this matter?”

lines.speaker: The Strange Gentleman
lines.text: “If I may give an opinion,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: remarked the strange gentleman,

lines.speaker: The Strange Gentleman
lines.text: “we’ve had just a little too much secrecy over this business already. For my part, I should like all Europe and America to hear the rights of it.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He was a small, wiry, sunburnt man, clean-shaven, with a sharp face and alert manner.

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Then I’ll tell our story right away,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the lady.

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Frank here and I met in ’84, in McQuire’s camp, near the Rockies, where Pa was working a claim. We were engaged to each other, Frank and I; but then one day father struck a rich pocket and made a pile, while poor Frank here had a claim that petered out and came to nothing. The richer Pa grew the poorer was Frank; so at last Pa wouldn’t hear of our engagement lasting any longer, and he took me away to ’Frisco. Frank wouldn’t throw up his hand, though; so he followed me there, and he saw me without Pa knowing anything about it. It would only have made him mad to know, so we just fixed it all up for ourselves. Frank said that he would go and make his pile, too, and never come back to claim me until he had as much as Pa. So then I promised to wait for him to the end of time and pledged myself not to marry anyone else while he lived. ‘Why shouldn’t we be married right away, then,’ said he, ‘and then I will feel sure of you; and I won’t claim to be your husband until I come back?’ Well, we talked it over, and he had fixed it all up so nicely, with a clergyman all ready in waiting, that we just did it right there; and then Frank went off to seek his fortune, and I went back to Pa.”

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “The next I heard of Frank was that he was in Montana, and then he went prospecting in Arizona, and then I heard of him from New Mexico. After that came a long newspaper story about how a miners’ camp had been attacked by Apache Indians, and there was my Frank’s name among the killed. I fainted dead away, and I was very sick for months after. Pa thought I had a decline and took me to half the doctors in ’Frisco. Not a word of news came for a year and more, so that I never doubted that Frank was really dead. Then Lord St. Simon came to ’Frisco, and we came to London, and a marriage was arranged, and Pa was very pleased, but I felt all the time that no man on this earth would ever take the place in my heart that had been given to my poor Frank.”

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Still, if I had married Lord St. Simon, of course I’d have done my duty by him. We can’t command our love, but we can our actions. I went to the altar with him with the intention to make him just as good a wife as it was in me to be. But you may imagine what I felt when, just as I came to the altar rails, I glanced back and saw Frank standing and looking at me out of the first pew. I thought it was his ghost at first; but when I looked again there he was still, with a kind of question in his eyes, as if to ask me whether I were glad or sorry to see him. I wonder I didn’t drop. I know that everything was turning round, and the words of the clergyman were just like the buzz of a bee in my ear. I didn’t know what to do. Should I stop the service and make a scene in the church? I glanced at him again, and he seemed to know what I was thinking, for he raised his finger to his lips to tell me to be still. Then I saw him scribble on a piece of paper, and I knew that he was writing me a note. As I passed his pew on the way out I dropped my bouquet over to him, and he slipped the note into my hand when he returned me the flowers. It was only a line asking me to join him when he made the sign to me to do so. Of course I never doubted for a moment that my first duty was now to him, and I determined to do just whatever he might direct.”

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “When I got back I told my maid, who had known him in California, and had always been his friend. I ordered her to say nothing, but to get a few things packed and my ulster ready. I know I ought to have spoken to Lord St. Simon, but it was dreadful hard before his mother and all those great people. I just made up my mind to run away and explain afterwards. I hadn’t been at the table ten minutes before I saw Frank out of the window at the other side of the road. He beckoned to me and then began walking into the Park. I slipped out, put on my things, and followed him. Some woman came talking something or other about Lord St. Simon to me—seemed to me from the little I heard as if he had a little secret of his own before marriage also—but I managed to get away from her and soon overtook Frank. We got into a cab together, and away we drove to some lodgings he had taken in Gordon Square, and that was my true wedding after all those years of waiting. Frank had been a prisoner among the Apaches, had escaped, came on to ’Frisco, found that I had given him up for dead and had gone to England, followed me there, and had come upon me at last on the very morning of my second wedding.”

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “I saw it in a paper,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: explained the American.

lines.speaker: Lord St. Simon
lines.text: “It gave the name and the church but not where the lady lived.”

lines.speaker: The Lady
lines.text: “Then we had a talk as to what we should do, and Frank was all for openness, but I was so ashamed of it all that I felt as if I should like to vanish away and never see any of them again—just sending a line to Pa, perhaps, to show him that I was alive. It was awful to me to think of all those lords and ladies sitting round that breakfast-table and waiting for me to come back. So Frank took my wedding-clothes and things and made a bundle of them, so that I should not be traced, and dropped them away somewhere where no one could find them. It is likely that we should have gone on to Paris to-morrow, only that this good gentleman, Mr. Holmes, came round to us this evening, though how he found us is more than I can think, and he showed us very clearly and kindly that I was wrong and that Frank was right, and that we should be putting ourselves in the wrong if we were so secret. Then he offered to give us a chance of talking to Lord St. Simon alone, and so we came right away round to his rooms at once. Now, Robert, you have heard it all, and I am very sorry if I have given you pain, and I hope that you do not think very meanly of me.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Lord St. Simon had by no means relaxed his rigid attitude, but had listened with a frowning brow and a compressed lip to this long narrative.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Excuse me,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “but it is not my custom to discuss my most intimate personal affairs in this public manner.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Then you won’t forgive me? You won’t shake hands before I go?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Oh, certainly, if it would give you any pleasure.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He put out his hand and coldly grasped that which she extended to him.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “I had hoped,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: suggested Holmes,

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “that you would have joined us in a friendly supper.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I think that there you ask a little too much,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: responded his Lordship.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I may be forced to acquiesce in these recent developments, but I can hardly be expected to make merry over them. I think that with your permission I will now wish you all a very good-night.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He included us all in a sweeping bow and stalked out of the room.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Then I trust that you at least will honour me with your company,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Sherlock Holmes.

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “It is always a joy to meet an American, Mr. Moulton, for I am one of those who believe that the folly of a monarch and the blundering of a minister in far-gone years will not prevent our children from being some day citizens of the same world-wide country under a flag which shall be a quartering of the Union Jack with the Stars and Stripes.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “The case has been an interesting one,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: remarked Holmes when our visitors had left us,

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “because it serves to show very clearly how simple the explanation may be of an affair which at first sight seems to be almost inexplicable. Nothing could be more natural than the sequence of events as narrated by this lady, and nothing stranger than the result when viewed, for instance, by Mr. Lestrade of Scotland Yard.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “You were not yourself at fault at all, then?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “From the first, two facts were very obvious to me, the one that the lady had been quite willing to undergo the wedding ceremony, the other that she had repented of it within a few minutes of returning home. Obviously something had occurred during the morning, then, to cause her to change her mind. What could that something be? She could not have spoken to anyone when she was out, for she had been in the company of the bridegroom. Had she seen someone, then? If she had, it must be someone from America because she had spent so short a time in this country that she could hardly have allowed anyone to acquire so deep an influence over her that the mere sight of him would induce her to change her plans so completely. You see we have already arrived, by a process of exclusion, at the idea that she might have seen an American. Then who could this American be, and why should he possess so much influence over her? It might be a lover; it might be a husband. Her young womanhood had, I knew, been spent in rough scenes and under strange conditions. So far I had got before I ever heard Lord St. Simon’s narrative. When he told us of a man in a pew, of the change in the bride’s manner, of so transparent a device for obtaining a note as the dropping of a bouquet, of her resort to her confidential maid, and of her very significant allusion to claim-jumping—which in miners’ parlance means taking possession of that which another person has a prior claim to—the whole situation became absolutely clear. She had gone off with a man, and the man was either a lover or was a previous husband—the chances being in favour of the latter.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “And how in the world did you find them?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “It might have been difficult, but friend Lestrade held information in his hands the value of which he did not himself know. The initials were, of course, of the highest importance, but more valuable still was it to know that within a week he had settled his bill at one of the most select London hotels.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “How did you deduce the select?”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “By the select prices. Eight shillings for a bed and eightpence for a glass of sherry pointed to one of the most expensive hotels. There are not many in London which charge at that rate. In the second one which I visited in Northumberland Avenue, I learned by an inspection of the book that Francis H. Moulton, an American gentleman, had left only the day before, and on looking over the entries against him, I came upon the very items which I had seen in the duplicate bill. His letters were to be forwarded to 226 Gordon Square; so thither I travelled, and being fortunate enough to find the loving couple at home, I ventured to give them some paternal advice and to point out to them that it would be better in every way that they should make their position a little clearer both to the general public and to Lord St. Simon in particular. I invited them to meet him here, and, as you see, I made him keep the appointment.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “But with no very good result,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: I remarked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “His conduct was certainly not very gracious.”

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “Ah, Watson,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Holmes, smiling,

lines.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
lines.text: “perhaps you would not be very gracious either, if, after all the trouble of wooing and wedding, you found yourself deprived in an instant of wife and of fortune. I think that we may judge Lord St. Simon very mercifully and thank our stars that we are never likely to find ourselves in the same position. Draw your chair up and hand me my violin, for the only problem we have still to solve is how to while away these bleak autumnal evenings.”
